The Problem Turnitin Was Built to Solve

Every year, hundreds of millions of students submit written work across a digitally connected, globalised education system. As access to information has expanded, so has the temptation — and the ease — of presenting another's work, or a machine's output, as one's own.

Turnitin was designed to answer a simple but consequential question: is this piece of writing genuinely original? It does this not through human judgment alone, but through an automated system built on comparison at a scale no single examiner could achieve.

03 / 12

How the System Actually Works

  1. It cross-references submitted text against a repository of billions of academic papers, journals, websites, and previously submitted student work — producing a similarity score, not a guilt verdict.
  2. A newer layer attempts to detect AI-generated writing by identifying statistical patterns — unusually uniform sentence rhythm, predictable word choice — that are more characteristic of machine output than deliberate proof of authorship.
04 / 12

Inside the Report: Core Features

Similarity Score

An overall percentage showing how much submitted text matches existing sources, color-graded from low to high overlap.

Source Breakdown

Every matched passage is linked to its originating document — a journal article, a website, or another student's prior submission.

AI Writing Indicator

A separate percentage estimating how much of the text may be AI-generated, based on stylistic and statistical patterns.

Exclusion Settings

Instructors can exclude quotes, bibliographies, and small matches, so the score reflects substantive overlap rather than formatting.

Key References & Student AI Usage

Reference Point 1

Turnitin (2023) reports that AI-writing indicators are informational tools, not definitive proof of academic misconduct — instructors must apply judgement.

Reference Point 2

COPE guidelines state that using AI tools to assist in writing is permissible as long as it is disclosed and the student remains accountable for the work.

Reference Point 3

Stanford HAI (2023) highlights that the line between AI-assisted and AI-generated work is context-dependent and must be evaluated with supporting evidence.

Student AI Usage Reality

89% of students have used AI tools at least once for academic work. Of these, 63% use AI for editing & structuring only — while retaining their own original ideas and arguments. Only 17% use AI to generate complete content.

Section VI - Redundant Publication

Definition Redundant publication occurs when two or more papers, without full cross-reference, share the same hypothesis, data, discussion points, or conclusions.
Action 2

Prior publication of an abstract at a conference does not preclude later submission, but full disclosure must be made at the time of submission.

Action 3

Re-publication in another language is acceptable only with full, prominent disclosure of the original source.

Action 4

Authors must disclose related or similar papers, even in a different language or still in press, at the time of submission.

11 / 12

Section V - Dealing with Misconduct

Sanctions Possible editorial actions for redundant publication or plagiarism include:
Sanction 5

Publication of a notice of redundant publication or plagiarism.

Sanction 6

An editorial giving full details of the misconduct.

Sanction 8

Formal withdrawal or retraction of the paper from the scientific literature, informing other editors and indexing authorities.
